bib.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v4, 19 Feb 2014; ICLR 2014 per ledger)

question: Do individual high-level units carry the semantics of a deep network, and is the network's input-output map smooth under small input perturbations?
hypothesis: Implied: networks that generalise well should be locally smooth, so imperceptible perturbations should not change the class; the paper finds otherwise.
contributions: Random directions in feature space are as semantically interpretable as individual units (section 3).
Adversarial examples: imperceptible perturbations found by optimisation that change the prediction (section 4).
Adversarial examples transfer across models and across disjoint training sets (section 4.2).
Spectral (Lipschitz upper bound) analysis of layer instability (section 4.3).

method.summary: Finds minimum-L2 perturbations r with f(x+r)=l by box-constrained L-BFGS with a line search on c, on MNIST (FC, autoencoder), AlexNet and QuocNet. Measures how often the perturbed images fool other models and models trained on disjoint data, and computes upper Lipschitz bounds per layer of AlexNet.
method.task: adversarial example generation and transfer for image classifiers; unit analysis

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.split: split into disjoint P1 and P2 of 30000 each for the cross-training-set test; Table 4 distorts the test set

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.split: validation set used as I for unit analysis

models.name: FC10(lambda)
models.architecture: softmax linear classifier on pixels, lambda 1e-4, 1e-2, 1

models.name: FC100-100-10 / FC200-200-10 / FC123-456-10
models.architecture: sigmoid network with two hidden layers and softmax classifier

models.name: AE400-10
models.architecture: single-layer sparse autoencoder with sigmoid, 400 nodes, plus softmax; first layer not fine-tuned

models.name: QuocNet
models.architecture: unsupervised network; binary car classifier trained on last-layer features without fine-tuning

training.objective: MNIST models: softmax cross-entropy plus quadratic weight decay lambda*sum(w_i^2)/k, k = units in the layer

other.adversarial training: 2-layer 100-100-10 net trained with a pool of adversarial examples, a random subset continuously replaced by new ones and mixed into the training set; adversarial examples generated for each layer's outputs and used to train all layers above; pool kept per layer; alternating training; pool size and mix ratio not stated
other.AlexNet/QuocNet training: not described; pretrained models of Krizhevsky 2012 and Le 2011 used

inference.samples: adversarial example for every sample; Fig 5 AlexNet examples strictly randomly chosen, 64 examples for average distortion

parameters.attack: minimise ||r||_2 s.t. f(x+r)=l, x+r in [0,1]^m, approximated by box-constrained L-BFGS minimising c|r| + loss_f(x+r,l) with line search for minimum c>0 that gives f(x+r)=l
parameters.amplification: x + 0.1*(x'-x)/||x'-x||_2 raises distortion by about 40%, stddev 0.06 to 0.1

metrics.name: Error rate on distorted examples
metrics.definition: proportion of adversarial instances misclassified by a given model

metrics.name: Average minimum distortion
metrics.definition: sqrt(sum_i (x'_i - x_i)^2 / n), n=784, pixel range [0,1]; minimum average needed to reach 0% accuracy on the training set

eval.protocol: Single runs, no seeds, no significance tests reported. Table 2 distorts training set; Table 4 distorts test set.

Training on a pool of adversarial examples gave a 100-100-10 net with test error below 1.2%, versus 1.6% with weight decay alone and about 1.3% with dropout.

results.quote: test error below 1.2% by keeping a pool of adversarial examples a random subset

results.claim: Upper Lipschitz bound of AlexNet conv layer 2 is 10 and of conv layer 5 is 11; bounds are large from the first layer on.
results.setup: AlexNet of Krizhevsky 2012, frame bounds computed via eq (1)
results.table: Table 5, row Conv. 5, column Upper bound
results.note: Upper bounds only: large bounds do not imply adversarial examples exist, small ones would guarantee none.

results.claim: Unit-level and random-direction images both give semantically coherent sets, so the natural basis is not special.
results.setup: MNIST and AlexNet, held-out set I
results.quote: This suggests that the natural basis is not better than a random basis for inspecting the properties

limits: Authors concede they do not understand how often adversarial negatives appear: 'we don't have a deep understanding of how often adversarial negatives appears'.
Quantitative transfer results are on MNIST fully connected nets only; no convolutional MNIST results, AlexNet only qualitative.
Adversarial-training result is preliminary; pool size, ratio, iterations and seeds are not given.
Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not explain transfer across models or training sets.
Attack is white-box and optimisation-based (L-BFGS), costly; fast gradient methods came later.
No defence or training hyperparameters (c, iterations) given for the attack; no code released.

terms.definition: imperceptible non-random perturbation applied to a test image that arbitrarily changes the network's prediction, found by optimizing the input to maximize the prediction error
the closest image to x classified as l by f, a minimizer of ||r||_2 with f(x+r)=l and x+r in [0,1]^m
a relatively large fraction of examples will be misclassified by networks trained from scratch with different hyper-parameters
a relatively large fraction of examples will be misclassified by networks trained from scratch on a disjoint training set
